Please review the following document.

<document>
Policy Brief: Scaling High-Dose Tutoring in Year 7 Mathematics
Riverside County Education Authority, Policy Unit, January 2026

Summary
In 2024-25 the Authority funded a pilot of high-dose mathematics tutoring for Year 7 pupils in six urban secondary schools. Pupils who received tutoring made substantially more progress than a randomly selected comparison group. This brief recommends extending the programme to all 42 secondary schools in the county from September 2026, at an estimated annual cost of £2.9 million.

The pilot
Tutoring was delivered in groups of three pupils, three one-hour sessions a week, for 30 weeks, during the school day. Tutors were undergraduate and postgraduate students from Riverside University, recruited, trained and paid £16 an hour through the University's Education Department. Pupils were eligible if they had scored below the expected standard in the end-of-primary mathematics assessment.

Of 480 eligible pupils in the six schools, 360 were offered places by lottery, because tutor capacity was limited; the remaining 120 formed the comparison group. Because places were allocated at random, the comparison is a fair one: the two groups had near-identical prior attainment, attendance and demographic profiles at the start of the year.

Results
Progress was measured using the standardised Year 7 mathematics assessment, taken in September 2024 and again in June 2025.

Group | Pupils assessed in June | Mean score, Sept 2024 | Mean score, June 2025 | Gain
Tutored | 342 | 88.0 | 98.6 | 10.6
Comparison | 114 | 87.8 | 93.4 | 5.6

Tutored pupils gained 10.6 points against 5.6 for the comparison group, a gain 89% larger. The difference of five points is equivalent to roughly four months of additional progress, and is in line with the effects reported in the national evidence base for small-group tutoring. Attendance at sessions averaged 87%, and 95% of the pupils offered a place completed the programme.

Teachers in all six schools reported that tutored pupils were more confident in lessons, and four of the six head teachers have asked for the programme to continue.

Proposal
We propose to extend the programme to all eligible Year 7 pupils in the county's 42 secondary schools from September 2026, retaining the design that proved effective: the one-to-one format used in the pilot, three sessions a week for 30 weeks, delivered in school hours by trained university-student tutors. Riverside University has agreed in principle to expand its recruitment, and its Education Department will continue to train and pay tutors.

Around 3,100 pupils a year meet the eligibility criterion across the 42 schools. Of these schools, 26 are in the county's rural districts, between 40 and 75 miles from the University campus; the remaining 16 are in or near Riverside itself, within a short bus ride of the campus, as were all six pilot schools.

Cost
The pilot cost £750 per tutored pupil: £480 in tutor pay (90 hours of tutoring per group, shared among three pupils, at £16 an hour), £220 for university coordination and training, and £50 for materials and assessment. Applying the pilot unit cost to 3,100 pupils gives an annual cost of £2.9 million.

This compares favourably with the Authority's current spending on Year 8 and Year 9 catch-up classes, which cost £1,100 per pupil and have shown no measurable effect on attainment in the last two internal evaluations. We propose that the catch-up budget be wound down over two years and the savings redirected to tutoring.

Risks and mitigations
Tutor quality. All tutors will complete the University's 12-hour training course and be observed twice per term by a school mathematics lead.
Timetabling. Sessions will be scheduled during form time and one weekly mathematics lesson, as in the pilot, so pupils do not miss other subjects.
Evaluation. The Policy Unit will continue to track progress using the standardised assessment and will report to Committee annually.

Recommendation
The pilot provides rigorous, randomised evidence that high-dose tutoring substantially accelerates progress for pupils who start secondary school behind in mathematics. The model is proven and its costs are known. We recommend that the Committee approve £2.9 million a year from September 2026 to extend tutoring to all 42 secondary schools, funded in part by winding down the catch-up class budget.
</document>
response:
# Review: Policy Brief on Scaling High-Dose Tutoring in Year 7 Mathematics

The pilot evidence looks sound. The randomised design, balanced groups, similar attrition in both arms (95%), and an effect consistent with the national literature make a credible case that the programme worked in those six schools. The problems are in the proposal. It doesn't match the pilot it claims to replicate, the costing doesn't add up, and it plans a rollout to settings the pilot never tested. Below are the issues, most serious first.

## 1. The proposal describes a different programme from the pilot

- **Pilot:** "groups of three pupils"
- **Proposal:** "retaining the design that proved effective: the one-to-one format used in the pilot"

This contradiction needs resolving before the Committee votes, because the two formats differ greatly in cost and in evidence:

- **If one-to-one is intended**, the pilot doesn't support it, and the cost changes sharply. Tutor pay becomes 90 hours × £16 = £1,440 per pupil instead of £480. That is about £1,710 per pupil in total, or roughly **£5.3m a year** for 3,100 pupils, and it needs three times as many tutors.
- **If groups of three are intended**, which is likely, the word "one-to-one" must be corrected. Otherwise the Committee may approve something different from what is costed.

## 2. The cost total is wrong

The brief's own figures are £750 per pupil × 3,100 pupils = **£2.325m**, not £2.9m. £2.9m implies about £935 per pupil. Either there is an arithmetic error or there are uncosted elements, such as rural travel or extra coordination, that should be listed. As written, the brief says "its costs are known" while its headline figure can't be reproduced from its own numbers.

## 3. The pilot doesn't cover most of the proposed rollout

- All six pilot schools were urban, "within a short bus ride of the campus."
- 26 of the 42 target schools (62%) are rural, **40–75 miles** from the University.
- Tutors are students, and sessions run in school hours, three times a week.

The brief doesn't explain how students will reach rural schools three times a week alongside their own studies. A 40–75 mile trip each way makes a one-hour session take most of a day. Options include online delivery, locally recruited tutors, or travel stipends. Each would change the cost, the tutor pool, or the format, and none was tested in the pilot. Travel and time costs are also missing from the budget.

The "Risks and mitigations" section doesn't mention this, even though it is probably the largest risk in the proposal.

## 4. The scale-up in tutor supply is large and unaddressed

- **Pilot:** 360 pupils ÷ 3 = 120 groups × 3 hours = **~360 tutor-hours a week**
- **Proposal:** 3,100 ÷ 3 ≈ 1,035 groups × 3 hours = **~3,100 tutor-hours a week**, about 8.6 times the pilot

The University has agreed only "in principle." The brief should say how many tutors are needed, whether the University can supply them, and what happens if it can't. Quality and the observation regime (two observations per term by school maths leads, now covering hundreds of tutors) also need to be shown to hold at that scale.

## 5. The Recommendation overclaims

"The model is proven and its costs are known" goes beyond the evidence:

- The evidence is one cohort, one year, six urban schools, and one delivery partner.
- There is no follow-up on whether the gains persist into Year 8.
- The costs don't reconcile (point 2) and leave out rural delivery (point 3).

A fairer statement would be that the pilot gives strong evidence of effectiveness in urban schools near the University, and that the main open questions are rural delivery and tutor supply at scale.

## 6. The evaluation plan loses the ability to measure impact

If every eligible pupil is tutored, there is no comparison group. Annual tracking of scores alone can't tell whether the programme still works at scale or in rural schools. A **phased rollout** would solve this and also reduce delivery risk. For example, schools could be randomised into a 2026 or 2027 start, or rural schools could start with a randomised trial of whichever delivery model is chosen.

## 7. Winding down catch-up classes needs more detail

- The Year 8/9 catch-up classes serve different pupils from Year 7 tutoring. Winding them down removes support from current Year 8/9 pupils, who would never receive tutoring. The brief should say so.
- The catch-up budget isn't stated, so the Committee can't see how much of the £2.9m it covers or what the net new cost is.
- Two internal evaluations showing no effect is a reasonable case for change. It would help to state their design and sample sizes.

## 8. Smaller points

- **"Four months of additional progress":** state the effect size (the 5-point difference in standard-deviation units) and the conversion used, so readers can check it against the national evidence.
- **Completion rate:** "95% of the pupils offered a place completed the programme" matches the 342 of 360 assessed in June. Confirm that these are the same measure; being assessed is not the same as completing.
- **Head teacher support:** "four of the six head teachers have asked for the programme to continue" implies two did not. Briefly explaining why would be more convincing than leaving the gap.
- **Teacher reports of confidence** are anecdotal and unblinded. They are fine as colour but shouldn't sit under "Results" next to the trial outcome.
- **Timetabling:** three one-hour sessions from "form time and one weekly mathematics lesson" seems unlikely to add up, since form time is usually 20–30 minutes. Clarify where the hours come from, and note that pupils do miss a maths lesson.
- **Analysis method:** say whether results are intention-to-treat (all 360 offered places) or only for those assessed. With 95% follow-up in both arms this matters little, but a rigorous brief should state it.

## Suggested revisions

1. Fix the "one-to-one" error and confirm the group size.
2. Recompute the cost from stated unit costs and itemise any additions, including rural delivery.
3. Add a section on rural delivery and tutor supply, with numbers.
4. Replace the full immediate rollout with a phased, evaluable rollout, or at least justify not phasing.
5. State the catch-up budget and the net cost, and address the effect on Year 8/9 pupils.
6. Soften "proven" to match the evidence.

With these changes, the brief would rest on a strong pilot and avoid promising more than that pilot can support.
